faq.q: Can therapeutic endoscopy be done without anaesthesia?

faq.a: Use the next safest option (e.g., injection alone for ulcer bleeding) and arrange transfer if perforation risk is high.
faq.q: What if a required endoscopic device is unavailable?

faq.a: Start non‑selective beta‑blockers and treat underlying portal hypertension; schedule repeat endoscopy in 2‑4 weeks.

exam: A patient with melena and hemoglobin 7 g/dL – what is the next immediate step? — Arrange urgent therapeutic upper endoscopy after cross‑matching blood.
How does Forrest classification guide endoscopic therapy? — Higher grades (Ia, Ib) need combined injection and thermal methods; lower grades may need only observation.
Why is band ligation preferred over sclerotherapy for esophageal varices in a hepatitis‑B patient? — Banding achieves mechanical hemostasis with fewer systemic complications.
A 45‑year‑old with a 2 cm sessile colonic polyp – which endoscopic technique is optimal and why? — Snare polypectomy with electrocautery; it removes the lesion completely and allows histology.
What red‑flag sign after therapeutic endoscopy mandates emergency surgery? — New onset peritonitis suggesting perforation.
If epinephrine injection alone is used for ulcer bleeding, what is the risk? — High re‑bleeding rate; combination therapy is required.
In a setting without a therapeutic endoscope, how would you manage active variceal bleed? — Use balloon tamponade (e.g., Sengstaken) as a bridge to transfer.
What follow‑up is required after successful polypectomy of a high‑risk adenoma? — Surveillance colonoscopy at 6‑12 months to detect recurrence.
ai.title: Therapeutic Endoscopy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Therapeutic endoscopy uses flexible scopes to treat gastrointestinal lesions at the bedside, crucial where surgery is limited. Understanding indications, technique, and complications helps clinicians act safely in low‑resource settings.

b: Diagnostic endoscopy + therapeutic intervention in one session
Requires visual confirmation of lesion before treatment
sections.p: Therapeutic endoscopy refers to endoscopic procedures that actively treat disease (e.g., bleeding control, polyp removal) rather than only visualise the lumen.

b: Forrest I (active spurting) → highest urgency
Forrest IIa (visible vessel) → high risk
Forrest III (clean base) → low risk
sections.p: Severity is judged by the lesion type and risk of re‑bleeding or perforation; common staging systems include Forrest classification for ulcer bleeding and Paris classification for polyps.

b: Peptic ulcer disease (H. pylori, NSAIDs, malaria‑related stress ulcer)
Variceal bleeding (portal hypertension from schistosomiasis, hepatitis B/C)
Colonic polyps (adenomatous, inflammatory from chronic infection)
Foreign body impaction (fish bone, herbal pill fragments)
sections.p: Lesions needing therapeutic endoscopy arise from common tropical conditions and routine pathology.

b: Hematemesis or melena → suspect upper GI source
Fresh rectal bleeding → consider lower GI source
Abdominal pain with vomiting → possible obstruction or perforation
sections.p: Patients present with overt GI bleeding, obstruction, or incidental lesions found on imaging.
Endoscopy itself provides diagnosis and therapy; adjunct tests guide urgency.

t.b: Is the bleed clinically significant? <8 g/dL prompts urgent endoscopy
Will transfusion be needed? Ensures blood is ready for high‑risk procedures
Detects portal hypertension or ascites when endoscopy unavailable
Confirms ongoing lower GI bleed if endoscopy delayed

b: Perforation – sudden severe pain, rigid abdomen
Aspiration – cough, desaturation during upper endoscopy
Severe bleeding – hypotension, tachycardia after therapy
sections.p: Complications are rare but can be life‑threatening; early recognition is vital.

b: Peptic ulcer bleeding → injection of epinephrine + thermal coagulation; avoid pure epinephrine alone
Variceal bleeding → band ligation; avoid sclerotherapy in cirrhosis with severe coagulopathy
Polyp removal → snare polypectomy; avoid hot biopsy forceps for large lesions
Foreign body → retrieval net; avoid blind forceps that may push object deeper
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then apply the appropriate endoscopic technique.

b: Repeat hemoglobin at 6 h and 24 h
PPIs for ulcer disease, beta‑blockers for varices
Surveillance endoscopy in 6‑12 months for high‑risk polyps
sections.p: After therapeutic endoscopy, monitor for re‑bleeding and arrange secondary prevention.

b: Mallory‑Weiss tear – superficial mucosal laceration, treated conservatively
Diverticular bleed – usually stops spontaneously, may need clipping not banding
sections.p: Conditions that mimic GI bleeding but need different management.

b: Normal hemoglobin early in massive bleed – compensate until later drop
Negative stool occult blood after recent massive bleed – dilution effect
sections.p: Certain findings may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain after endoscopy
Massive hematemesis or melena with hemodynamic instability
